In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the role of hypoxic sensing and signaling in the development of cancer, (2) the role of HIF-1alpha as a master switch in the hypoxia response and its regulation by post-translational modifications, (3) the role of reactive oxygen species and redox regulation in the HIF pathway, (4) the role of oxygen sensing in the control of cell proliferation, (5) oxygen sensing and signaling in stem cells and their differentiation, and
the molecular mechanisms that allow cells to sense oxygen, to adapt to hypoxia, and to respond to the hypoxic environment in a manner that allows them to survive and thrive.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the field of hypoxia research is in a state of flux.
the HIF pathway and the cellular response to hypoxia have been well studied in many organisms and that the results are applicable in many ways to human health and disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have learned that the HIF pathway is a key mediator of the cellular response to oxygen deprivation, but that there are multiple layers of control and that there are other pathways involved.
hypoxia is an important signal that can lead to a variety of adaptive responses, ranging from changes in gene expression, to altered cellular behavior, to the development of new blood vessels.
we are learning to "think outside the cell" by studying the molecular mechanisms that allow animals to survive and thrive in a variety of hypoxic environments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIFs, the key transcription factors involved in oxygen sensing, can be regulated in a variety of ways.
the HIF signaling pathway is a major hub for cellular adaptation to low-oxygen environments, and that this pathway is conserved from bacteria to mammals, including humans.
hypoxic adaptation is not only a "critter thing" but also a "cancer thing."
